items.question_text: Your startup has never implemented a formal security policy. Currently, everyone in the company has access to the datasets stored in Google BigQuery. Teams have freedom to use the service as they see fit, and they have not documented their use cases. You have been asked to secure the data warehouse. You need to discover what everyone is doing. What should you do first?
items.solution_text:
To discover what users are actually doing with the data, you must review access patterns and query history, which is provided by Google Cloud Audit Logs (formerly Stackdriver).
Audit logs record specific user actions, such as who accessed which datasets and tables, providing the necessary visibility to establish a baseline before implementing restrictions.
Options B, C, and D provide static permissions, computational resource usage, or billing data, none of which reveal actual user behavior or data access history.

choices.text: Use Google Stackdriver Audit Logs to review data access.
Get the identity and access management IIAM) policy of each table
Use Stackdriver Monitoring to see the usage of BigQuery query slots.
Use the Google Cloud Billing API to see what account the warehouse is being billed to.

items.question_text: Your company is migrating their 30-node Apache Hadoop cluster to the cloud. They want to re-use Hadoop jobs they have already created and minimize the management of the cluster as much as possible. They also want to be able to persist data beyond the life of the cluster. What should you do?
items.solution_text:
Cloud Dataproc is the managed service designed to run existing Hadoop and Spark jobs with minimal cluster management overhead. By using the Google Cloud Storage connector instead of local HDFS, data persists in Cloud Storage independently of the cluster's lifecycle, satisfying the requirement for long-term data retention.
Option A (Dataflow) requires rewriting jobs, while Options C and E involve self-managed Compute Engine instances.

choices.text: Create a Google Cloud Dataflow job to process the data.
Create a Google Cloud Dataproc cluster that uses persistent disks for HDFS.
Create a Hadoop cluster on Google Compute Engine that uses persistent disks.
Create a Cloud Dataproc cluster that uses the Google Cloud Storage connector.
Create a Hadoop cluster on Google Compute Engine that uses Local SSD disks.

items.question_text: Business owners at your company have given you a database of bank transactions. Each row contains the user ID, transaction type, transaction location, and transaction amount. They ask you to investigate what type of machine learning can be applied to the data. Which three machine learning applications can you use? (Choose three.)
items.solution_text:
Unsupervised learning is suitable for fraud detection (B) when historical data lacks explicit labels for fraudulent transactions, allowing the model to identify anomalies or outliers.
Clustering (C) is an unsupervised technique that groups transactions based on feature similarity, such as amount and location patterns, without predefined categories.
Supervised learning can predict transaction locations (D) because the dataset contains labeled historical data linking user IDs and transaction types to specific geographic outcomes.

choices.text: Supervised learning to determine which transactions are most likely to be fraudulent.
Unsupervised learning to determine which transactions are most likely to be fraudulent.
Clustering to divide the transactions into N categories based on feature similarity.
Supervised learning to predict the location of a transaction.
Reinforcement learning to predict the location of a transaction.
Unsupervised learning to predict the location of a transaction.

items.question_text: Your company's on-premises Apache Hadoop servers are approaching end-of-life, and IT has decided to migrate the cluster to Google Cloud Dataproc. A like-for- like migration of the cluster would require 50 TB of Google Persistent Disk per node. The CIO is concerned about the cost of using that much block storage. You want to minimize the storage cost of the migration. What should you do?
items.solution_text: Google Cloud Dataproc is designed to use Google Cloud Storage (GCS) for primary data storage, which eliminates the need for expensive local Persistent Disks on every node. GCS offers significantly lower costs per TB compared to block storage and scales automatically without manual provisioning. Using preemptible VMs (Option B) reduces compute costs but does not address the high cost of the required 50 TB of storage per node.

choices.text: Put the data into Google Cloud Storage.
Use preemptible virtual machines (VMs) for the Cloud Dataproc cluster.
Tune the Cloud Dataproc cluster so that there is just enough disk for all data.
Migrate some of the cold data into Google Cloud Storage, and keep only the hot data in Persistent Disk.

items.question_text:
You work for a car manufacturer and have set up a data pipeline using Google Cloud Pub/Sub to capture anomalous sensor events. You are using a push subscription in Cloud Pub/Sub that calls a custom HTTPS endpoint that you have created to take action of these anomalous events as they occur. Your custom
HTTPS endpoint keeps getting an inordinate amount of duplicate messages. What is the most likely cause of these duplicate messages?
items.solution_text:
Google Cloud Pub/Sub guarantees at-least-once delivery and redelivers messages if the push endpoint fails to send a valid HTTP 200 response within the acknowledgement deadline.
If the custom endpoint does not acknowledge messages in time, Pub/Sub treats them as unprocessed and retries delivery, resulting in duplicates.

choices.text: The message body for the sensor event is too large.
Your custom endpoint has an out-of-date SSL certificate.
The Cloud Pub/Sub topic has too many messages published to it.
Your custom endpoint is not acknowledging messages within the acknowledgement deadline.
